summary: Specifies how Multicast VPN (MVPN) can use Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER) to carry multicast traffic across a provider backbone. BIER provides efficient multicast forwarding through a domain without intermediate routers keeping per-flow state. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending the same video to many viewers can burden the routers in between. BIER stamps each packet with a list of who needs it, so the routers just copy it to the right places without remembering each show.

questions: what is the pmsi tunnel attribute
subtitle: How a provider carries customer multicast across its backbone with BIER, using BGP routes to advertise it and an MPLS label to sort it.

tldr.problem: Multicast VPN service needs P-tunnels across the provider backbone, and BIER forwards multicast without per-flow state or tree building but has no explicit tunnels for the MVPN procedures to name.
tldr.mechanism: BIER is treated as a tunnel type (0x0B) in the PMSI Tunnel attribute, which carries a sub-domain, BFR-id and BFR-prefix plus an upstream-assigned MPLS label. Egress routers answer with Leaf A-D routes, and the ingress router builds the BIER BitString from them.
tldr.outcome: MVPN traffic of many VPNs can ride BIER, and BIER can serve as some or all segments of a segmented P-tunnel. Procedures for BIDIR-PIM customers are out of scope. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8556 is a Proposed Standard on the IETF Standards Track, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: MVPN Meets BIER
sections.content:
RFC 6513 and RFC 6514 let a Service Provider offer Multicast VPN (MVPN) service. Multicast tunnels called P-tunnels carry customer multicast across the backbone, and the specifications allow several kinds of P-tunnel technology.

Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER, RFC 8279) forwards multicast optimally through a multicast domain without per-flow state in intermediate routers and without an explicit tree-building protocol. This RFC specifies how MVPN uses BIER to carry traffic over the backbone.

BIER builds no tunnels, but you can picture one point-to-multipoint tunnel from each Bit Forwarding Ingress Router (BFIR) to all Bit Forwarding Egress Routers (BFERs) in the BIER domain. These implicit tunnels are not specific to any VPN, so the MVPN procedures for aggregating several VPNs on one P-tunnel are used. BIER only works inside one IGP domain, but MVPN P-tunnels can be segmented at ASBRs or ABRs, so BIER can provide some or all segments if the segmentation points can act as BFIRs and BFERs. Support for Bidirectional PIM customers is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone company already has a way to send group messages for its business customers. This RFC plugs in a newer, simpler delivery method that does not need each middle router to remember every group.

sections.title: The PMSI Tunnel Attribute for BIER
sections.content:
BGP routes announce a multicast service, called a PMSI, and the PMSI Tunnel attribute (PTA) on the route says which P-tunnel carries it. When BIER carries the PMSI, the BFIR builds the PTA. If P-tunnels are segmented, a segmentation point (a BFER) may replace the PTA with one for the next segment, and then acts as BFIR for that segment.

The PTA has these parts:

  • Tunnel Type: 0x0B, assigned by IANA for BIER. MVPN procedures treat BIER as if it were a tunnel type.
  • Tunnel Identifier: a one-octet BIER sub-domain-id, a two-octet BFR-id of the router building the PTA in that sub-domain, and that router's BFR-prefix, which is a /32 IPv4 or /128 IPv6 address (told apart by the PTA length).
  • MPLS Label: an upstream-assigned, non-zero label chosen by the BFIR.
  • Flags: two are meaningful, Leaf Information Required (LIR) and Leaf Information Required per Flow (LIR-pF).

A wrongly set Tunnel Identifier or label cannot be detected by the protocol and will cause improper delivery. A route with a BIER PTA MUST NOT be distributed beyond the BIER domain, which in practice is a requirement on how Route Targets are provisioned.
sections.plainLanguage: The announcement says which delivery method is used, who is sending, and which numbered sticker on each packet means which group. If you fill in the wrong sticker number, nothing warns you and the packets go to the wrong place.

sections.title: Rules for Choosing the MPLS Label
sections.content:
The label in the PTA is upstream-assigned. Two PTAs with the same BFR-prefix MUST use labels from the same label space. A BFIR MUST use different labels in the PTAs of two BIER routes when:

  • the routes do not carry the same set of Route Targets;
  • the routes have different Address Family Identifier values, so the egress PE can tell IPv4 from IPv6 payload by the label;
  • the BFIR is an ingress PE supporting MVPN extranet and the routes come from different VRFs, or only one route carries the Extranet Separation extended community;
  • segmented P-tunnels are used and the NLRIs of the routes are not identical.

The last rule lets a segmentation point switch packets from one P-tunnel segment to the next without other multicast forwarding state. If a segmentation point B1 replaces two incoming PTAs with new ones, the new labels MUST differ unless the routes share the same Originating Router, and the incoming BFR-prefixes and labels are also the same. B1 MUST program its data plane to swap the incoming label for its own and re-encapsulate in a BIER header carrying B1's BFR-id as BFIR-id.
sections.plainLanguage: Each group gets its own numbered sticker so the router at the other end knows exactly which group a packet belongs to, and the sticker must differ whenever the packets need to be treated differently.

sections.title: Finding the Receivers: Explicit Tracking
sections.content:
To build a BIER header, the BFIR must know which BFERs need each packet. There are two ways, both based on egress routers answering with Leaf A-D routes.

With the LIR flag (RFC 6513, RFC 6514), the BFIR MUST originate a (C-S,C-G) S-PMSI A-D route for the flow with a PTA that has the LIR flag set. BFERs that want the flow reply with (C-S,C-G) Leaf A-D routes, and matching them tells the BFIR the receiver set. If an I-PMSI or wildcard S-PMSI route with a BIER PTA already exists, the specific route MAY carry a PTA of tunnel type 'no tunnel information', which is equivalent to the less specific route's PTA.

With the optional LIR-pF flag (RFC 8534), the BFIR originates a wildcard S-PMSI A-D route with LIR-pF set, tunnel type BIER and a non-zero label. This can cut the number of S-PMSI routes to as few as one, a (C-*,C-*) route, but it gives no distinct label per flow, so it may be used only when segmented P-tunnels are not used. A BFIR MUST NOT use it unless it knows all the relevant BFERs support the flag, and a BFIR SHOULD NOT set the flag otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender first asks 'who wants this show?' and the interested routers raise their hands. The sender then knows exactly whose names to put on the list.

sections.title: Leaf A-D Routes from the Egress Router
sections.content:
Before an egress PE can receive a (C-S,C-G) flow over BIER, it needs a matching x-PMSI A-D route from the ingress PE whose PTA says BIER. That is either a (C-S,C-G) S-PMSI A-D route or a less specific route that is its match for reception under RFC 6625, excluding routes with no PTA or no tunnel type. Without a match it cannot receive the flow over BIER yet.

The egress PE then originates a Leaf A-D route whose PTA MUST be built like this: tunnel type BIER; MPLS label SHOULD be zero; sub-domain-id copied from the matching route's PTA; BFR-id set to the egress PE's BFR-id in that sub-domain; and BFR-prefix set to the egress PE's BFR-prefix. The ingress PE learns the egress BFR-prefix from this PTA and ignores the label field.
sections.plainLanguage: When a receiver wants a show, it sends back a note with its own address so the sender can add it to the delivery list.

sections.title: Data Plane: Sending and Receiving
sections.content:
The ingress PE finds the x-PMSI A-D route that matches a packet (RFC 6625). If its PTA says BIER, the upstream-assigned label from the PTA is pushed on the packet and the packet is wrapped in a BIER header, using the PTA's sub-domain. The BFIR finds the Leaf A-D routes corresponding to that S-PMSI route and uses the BFR-prefixes in them to build the BIER BitString. If a Leaf A-D route names a different sub-domain from the one used for sending, the bit for that BFER cannot be determined and it will not get the packet. The packet is then forwarded per RFC 8279 and RFC 8296.

When a BFER receives a packet, the BIER layer gives the multicast flow overlay the sub-domain-id and BFIR-id from the header and the payload, an MPLS packet whose top label is upstream-assigned. At an egress PE, the label, looked up in the context of the BFIR, identifies the egress VRF, and with the VRF's multicast state the PE decides which VRF interfaces to forward on. At a segmentation boundary, the label, which is distinct per C-flow, selects the next P-tunnel segment. A BFER can be both.
sections.plainLanguage: The first router puts the right sticker and the guest list on each packet. The routers in the middle just follow the list, and the last router uses the sticker to hand the packet to the right customer.

sections.title: Security Considerations and IANA
sections.content:
The procedures here do not, by themselves, provide privacy, integrity or authentication for the control plane or data plane. For BIER's security considerations the RFC points to RFC 8279 and RFC 8296, and for VPN technology to RFC 4364, RFC 6513 and RFC 6514.

The only IANA action is the assignment of codepoint 0x0B to BIER in the PMSI Tunnel Tunnel Types registry.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC does not add any locks of its own. It relies on the security of the systems it builds on.
